title: In and out
hook: some things hurry into being, others out, and the whole is a river (Meditations 6.15)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus's stepmother and mother, the duty and the home you keep returning to. Your line was visit the mother. Did you get your ten minutes? Day five hundred seventy-seven.

Stand at a hospital for one hour and you'd see it from both ends. On one floor, someone is born. On another, someone's family is saying goodbye. In the lobby, a man is buying flowers, and the flowers, already cut, have started to fade. Most days we only see one end at a time, so the whole thing stays invisible. Marcus Aurelius, in book six, tries to see both ends at once. Things arriving, things leaving, all the time.
screen: `A HOSPITAL, BOTH ENDS.` → `FLOWERS ALREADY FADING.` → `ARRIVING AND LEAVING AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Meditations six, fifteen, in George Long's translation, begins: "Some things are hurrying into existence, and others are hurrying out of it." Not drifting. Hurrying. The world is a doorway with traffic both ways. Second, the twist. Marcus adds that of what is coming into being, part is already gone. The new day starts ending at dawn. A song is partly over by its second verse. Arrival and departure aren't two events. They're one motion seen from two sides. Third, the sparrow. Then he asks: in a stream like this, where nothing stays, what passing thing would you set a high price on? He says it would be like falling in love with one of the sparrows flying past, and it's already out of sight. That can sound bleak. But read it slowly. He isn't saying don't love. He's saying don't stake your peace on holding any one sparrow still. Fourth, what to do with it. Seeing both ends at once is oddly steadying. When something you love arrives, you can greet it knowing it's passing, and so pay closer attention. When something you dread arrives, you know it's also already on its way out. Marcus doesn't ask you to stop caring. He asks you to care with your eyes open, the way you'd watch a sparrow: fully, and without trying to close your hand.
screen: `HURRYING IN, HURRYING OUT.` · `PART OF EVERY ARRIVAL IS GONE.` · `IN LOVE WITH A PASSING SPARROW.` · `CARE WITH YOUR EYES OPEN.` · then, large: `IN AND OUT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice your breath. Each breath is a tiny version of Marcus's sentence: air hurrying in, air hurrying out. Watch one breath begin. Watch it end. Then look around you, or listen. Find one thing that's beginning, a sound starting, light changing, a thought arriving. Find one thing that's ending. Hold both lightly, without grabbing either. In and out. The bell holds the time.
Marcus, who pictured the world as a doorway with traffic both ways, where even what arrives is already leaving. Today's word.
Your line: already out of sight. Today, notice one beginning and one ending, anywhere: a kettle starting to boil, a song finishing. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

screen: `DAY 577 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SCRATCH IN THE GYM.`

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus practice noticing beginnings and endings during the day, as a way to hold things they care about with attention rather than a tight grip.

myth: Marcus tells himself not to love anything
he warns against setting a high price on holding any passing thing still.
Marcus compares prizing passing things to falling in love with a sparrow flying by
and says it's already out of sight.
Meditations 6.15 says things drift slowly in and out of being
the word is hurrying, both ways.

fork.setup: something you love has just arrived: a visit, a season, a good stretch. by Marcus's picture, how do you hold it?
options: grip it hard so it can't leave.
refuse to enjoy it, since it will end.
enjoy it fully, knowing it's already passing.
fork.reveal: Meditations 6.15 sees arrival and departure as one motion; the sparrow is loved by watching, not by grabbing.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything ends, so why bother.
what it means: arrival and departure are one motion, so give full attention to what's passing through.
what a scholar hears: 6.15 sits in a run of entries on flux; Marcus's image of time as a river echoes Heraclitus, whom he names elsewhere in the Meditations.

sources.quoted: Some things are hurrying into existence, and others are hurrying out of it

notes: Confirm Long's wording of the opening of 6.15.
6.15: 'of that which is coming into existence part is already extinguished' and the sparrow image are paraphrased; confirm.
Heraclitus is named in the Meditations (e.g. 3.3, 4.46, 6.47); the river link is stated as an echo, not a quotation.
